title: A look at China's technology industry amid AI race with the U.S.
summary: Ahead of President Trump's visit to China, Geoff Bennett frames AI and US limits on advanced chips as the core tension between Washington and Beijing, and Nick Schifrin reports from Manila on new trade deals meant to balance Chinese influence before heading to Shenzhen. On Huawei's sprawling campus, Schifrin explains how the company survived US blacklisting by designing and linking its own chips, recovering its revenue with heavy state backing, and pushing into AI-driven cars that are increasingly built entirely in China. Analyst Michael Frank argues Huawei is Beijing's chosen AI flag-bearer, sheltered from US pressure by government money and a huge home market, and sees a winner-takes-all contest with Nvidia, whose board has just said it will not bring back Jensen Huang.
focus: Shadow Michael Frank's calm, single-speaker answer on why Huawei has the resources to keep competing, which ends on several useful idioms, then Schifrin's list-like tour of the campus's European look-alike buildings for rhythm and stress on place names.

vocab.meaning: a force or group that balances the power of another
vocab.context: Schifrin described the new group of US partners in Asia as a way to offset China's regional weight.
vocab.example: We positioned the regional distributor as a counterweight to the client's dependence on a single national retailer.

vocab.meaning: using pressure or threats to force someone to do something
vocab.context: Trump used it when arguing that no country should be at the mercy of one foreign supplier.
vocab.example: Diversifying suppliers protects the business from commercial coercion when a key vendor tries to dictate terms.

vocab.meaning: to hang over a situation as a threat or worry
vocab.context: Schifrin used it for the trade tensions hanging over Trump's meetings with Asian leaders.
vocab.example: The pending antitrust review looms over the merger timeline and makes the board reluctant to commit.

vocab.meaning: not stated directly, though the meaning is clear
vocab.context: Schifrin noted that a remark about supply chains was only thinly disguised criticism of Beijing.
vocab.example: The CEO's comment about legacy players was a barely veiled swipe at the market leader.

vocab.meaning: a company a government backs to lead its country in a strategic industry
vocab.zh: 国家冠军企业；国家扶持的龙头企业
vocab.context: Frank called Huawei the company Beijing has picked to lead its AI effort.
vocab.example: Competing against a national champion means pricing against a rival that never has to worry about funding.

vocab.meaning: involved with others in something wrong
vocab.context: In an archive clip, Pompeo warned firms against becoming partners in Huawei's alleged abuses.
vocab.example: The audit committee worried that ignoring the supplier's labour practices would make the company complicit.

vocab.meaning: able to manage without depending on others
vocab.zh: 自力更生的；自给自足的
vocab.context: Schifrin described Huawei's push to stop needing foreign chip technology.
vocab.example: The client wants its data platform to be self-reliant rather than locked into one cloud vendor.

vocab.meaning: to combine separate parts into one working whole
vocab.context: Schifrin explained that Huawei links many weaker chips to match more powerful foreign ones.
vocab.example: After three acquisitions, the team had to stitch together four billing systems into one customer view.

vocab.meaning: to make or develop something locally instead of importing it
vocab.context: Frank used it for China's effort to build its whole AI chip supply chain at home.
vocab.example: Several automakers are trying to indigenize battery production to cut exposure to import tariffs.

vocab.meaning: a place or market where new ideas or products are tried out
vocab.context: Frank said China's vast home market gives Huawei a place to trial its technology at scale.
vocab.example: We suggested using the Nordic stores as a test bed for the new pricing model before a full rollout.

vocab.meaning: describing a situation where one side's gain is exactly the other's loss
vocab.context: Frank described the US-China AI contest as one where only one side can win.
vocab.example: Framing the budget talks as zero-sum made each division defend its share instead of growing the pie.

vocab.meaning: to move goods secretly and illegally across borders
vocab.context: Schifrin mentioned Nvidia's promise to stop restricted chips being secretly moved to China.
vocab.example: The compliance review flagged resellers that might smuggle controlled components into sanctioned markets.

vocab.meaning: an event arranged mainly so people can be photographed together
vocab.context: Schifrin said the planned image of Trump, Putin and Xi together would serve Xi's goal of looking like a global stabiliser.
vocab.example: The signing ceremony was more photo-op than substance, since the key terms were still unresolved.

vocab.meaning: an area where one power has dominant control or sway
vocab.context: Schifrin noted Russian commentators comparing the summit to great powers dividing up the world.
vocab.example: Each regional head treated their territory as a sphere of influence, which blocked any shared sales strategy.

phrases.meaning: an essential, built-in part of something
phrases.context: Frank said Huawei's strategy is woven into China's national AI policy.
phrases.example: Regular stakeholder check-ins are part and parcel of any transformation programme we run.

phrases.meaning: to gain the benefits of something you or others did
phrases.context: Frank warned that whoever wins the global market will collect the payoff from AI.
phrases.example: Firms that invested in data infrastructure early are now reaping the rewards of faster AI adoption.

phrases.meaning: to try to solve something mainly by spending a lot
phrases.context: Frank suggested Beijing can keep pouring funds into Huawei's chip effort.
phrases.example: Throwing money at the problem won't fix churn if the onboarding experience stays broken.

phrases.meaning: to deal with problems someone else created
phrases.context: Schifrin used it for the task facing Nvidia's leadership after Huang's exit.
phrases.example: The new CFO spent her first year cleaning up the mess left by an aggressive acquisition spree.

phrases.meaning: to speak publicly for the first time after saying nothing
phrases.context: Bennett used it for Huang's first public statement since resigning.
phrases.example: The founder finally broke his silence on the restructuring in a memo to all staff.
